summary: SPHEREx Blink is an end-to-end discovery-to-clearinghouse platform that turns NASA SPHEREx’s billion-object sky survey into a live, crowd-powered observatory—unifying multi-epoch near-infrared analysis, machine-learning trajectory linking, and community peer review. Instead of requiring terabyte-scale downloads, the system streams targeted NASA/IPAC IRSA cutouts, subtracts Zodiacal light and Leave-One-Out median backgrounds, masks cosmic-ray and bad-pixel flags, and smoothly skips missing frames across all 6 detectors and 102 bands (0.75–5.00 µm). Simultaneously, our engine links moving targets using a Heuristic Tracker, a Random Forest classifier, and BLOOM saturated-centroid recovery—validated to 0.54 pixels on Comet 3I/ATLAS and 0.28 pixels on Asteroid (4) Vesta—while cross-matching Gaia DR3, AllWISE, CADC NEOSSat, and JPL Horizons. Through dual Volunteer and Scientist views featuring a 7-step guided tutorial, mobile layouts, and 102-band spectral curves for water, carbon dioxide, and silicates, users flag anomalies into a threaded Verification Feed. Reaching 10 community confirmations automatically validates astrometric residuals, dispatches IAU ADES or TNS packets to the Minor Planet Center, Transient Name Server, or AAVSO, and logs every accepted or rejected object in a persistent Candidate Catalogue—creating a scalable blueprint for turning petabyte space surveys into verified discoveries.
details:
Team Showerless created SPHERExBlink, an open-source web platform and machine-learning pipeline that makes NASA’s SPHEREx 102-band near-infrared sky survey available and actionable for professional astronomers and citizen-science volunteers. Instead of downloading monolithic full-sky FITS files, users can enter user-defined coordinates (e.g. Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis, interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS) to stream lightweight spatial cutouts via NASA IRSA and SPXQuery. The FastAPI backend calibrates each frame and median reference sky subtraction using Zodiacal light (ZODI), masks cosmic-ray and bad-pixel artifacts using FLAGS, and streams aligned epochs via Server-Sent Events in an interactive time-lapse viewer that skips gracefully over missing detector arrays (D1 to D6). In parallel, we apply a shift-and-stack track detector, integrating a Heuristic Leave-One-Out linearity filter and a Random Forest classifier, to identify moving candidates, tested to 0.54 pixels accuracy on comet 3I/ATLAS. Federated cone searches: cross-matching ESA Gaia DR3, NASA AllWISE, CDS SIMBAD and JPL Horizons to filter known sources. Built with TypeScript, React, Python, Docker, CI/CD and an offline auto-fallback state machine, EpochScan combines 102-band chemical spectrophotometry with a dual Volunteer and Scientist verification feed, shareable stateful URLs, an embed snippet generator, a data health diagnostics panel, and Astrop ready J2000 discovery dossiers.This is skyviewer in which the user will see his planet system:

Sky viewer serves as a collaborative peer-review space where users and scientists can inspect flagged moving objects, review exact observation settings, and verify astrometric tracks. It enables community discussion and validation of transient anomalies before candidates are officially processed.

The various tools used are:

1)The AI tool employs machine learning models—such as Random Forest classifiers and Heuristic Leave-One-Out (LOO) filters—to automatically detect, shift-and-stack, and rank moving object candidate tracks across multi-epoch frames. Here it is:

2) The chat and confirm tool is an interactive collaboratve platform that allows scientists and users to discuss, review, and formally validate flagged moving objects or transient candidates. It facilitates community consensus and expert verification before discoveries are logged or exported. Here it is:

3)The spectral analysis tool processes per-pixel wavelength data across the 102 infrared bands (utilizing FITS WCS-WAVE extensions) to plot flux versus wavelength, allowing researchers to evaluate material compositions like water ice, carbon dioxide, or silicates. Here it is:

4)We have also used infrared fliters that enable users to choose and isolate specific wavelength ranges across the six SPHEREx detectors bands (covering 0.75 µm to 5.00 µm over 102 channels) to investigate specific chemical signatures such as water ice, carbon dioxide, or silicates. We have also provided an option for image filtering that enables users to toggle options and allows users to switch between different processing views on the canvas such as raw aligned sky views, Zodiacal light (ZODI) subtracted clean views, or difference images to effectively isolate moving or transient objects.

ADDITIONAL FEATURE:

The share and embed feature generates unique links holding coordinates, area size, detector, and frame settings so anyone can instantly open the exact same view on any screen. Additionally, an embed button provides a short code snippet to easily paste the viewer into other websites, with images fetched fresh from NASA each time.

SPHERExBlink also provides two other major tools to help with user experience. SUch as:

1- The verification feed tool serves as a collaborative peer-review space where users and scientists can inspect flagged moving objects, review exact observation settings, and verify astrometric tracks. It enables community discussion and validation of transient anomalies before candidates are officially processed.

2- The candidate catalogue tool functions as an authoritative astronomical candidate registry, community consensus engine, and external clearinghouse submission portal. Once items are peer-reviewed and confirmed through the verification feed, they automatically index here and can be dispatched to official bodies like the MPC, TNS, or VSX.
